title: Landmark Study Links Rare Immune Cell Mutations to Autoimmune Disease, Opening Door to Precision Treatment
excerpt: Researchers at the Wellcome Sanger Institute used ultra-accurate DNA sequencing to discover that somatic mutations in B cells disable immune checkpoints in autoimmune thyroid disease, confirming a theory first proposed in the 1950s.
body:
• Scientists found that B cells in autoimmune thyroid patients accumulate somatic mutations that disable immune checkpoint genes TNFRSF14 and CD274 (PD-L1), allowing them to attack the body's own tissues
  • Using NanoSeq, an ultra-accurate sequencing method, researchers detected tens to hundreds of independently mutated B cell clones in highly inflamed thyroid biopsies
  • The discovery confirms the 'forbidden clone' hypothesis first proposed by Nobel laureate Frank Macfarlane Burnet in the 1950s
  • The findings could lead to targeted therapies for autoimmune diseases affecting 5-10% of the global population, replacing broad immunosuppression

Researchers at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals have produced the most compelling evidence yet that autoimmune diseases are driven by acquired DNA mutations in immune cells, a mechanism that mirrors the early stages of cancer but operates through a fundamentally different architecture.

The study, published in Nature in April 2026, used an ultra-accurate sequencing technique called NanoSeq to identify somatic mutations — DNA changes acquired during a person's lifetime, not inherited — in B cells from patients with autoimmune thyroid disease, including Hashimoto's and Graves' disease.

A 70-Year-Old Theory Confirmed

The idea that somatic mutations in immune cells might cause autoimmune disease was first proposed by Nobel laureate Frank Macfarlane Burnet in the 1950s. Burnet's "forbidden clone" hypothesis suggested that mutations could allow self-reactive immune cells to escape the body's tolerance checkpoints and attack healthy tissue. But the technology to detect such rare mutations in non-cancerous tissue did not exist until recently.

The Sanger team, led by Dr Pantelis Nicola and Dr Iñigo Martincorena, found that B cells in autoimmune thyroid tissue had convergently acquired loss-of-function mutations in two key immune checkpoint genes: TNFRSF14 (also known as HVEM) and CD274, which encodes PD-L1. These genes normally act as brakes on immune cell activity.

"This is a huge leap forward into the pathogenesis of autoimmune disease. It changes everything, and explains so much that was up in the air. It reminds me of when NASA fixed the optics on the Hubble Telescope: suddenly all the stars and galaxies are crystal clear."

— Professor Chris Goodnow, Garvan Institute and University of New South Wales Sydney

A Polyclonal Cascade

Unlike cancer, which typically begins with a single mutated cell that multiplies into a tumour, the researchers found that autoimmune disease involves a highly polyclonal process. In the most inflamed thyroid biopsies, they detected tens to hundreds of independently mutated B cell clones, each carrying different combinations of checkpoint mutations.

Some cells had accumulated as many as four to six driver mutations over many years, silently building up genetic changes before symptoms appeared. In one Hashimoto's thyroiditis sample, about 62% of profiled B cells carried mutations in TNFRSF14, with most having lost function in both copies of the gene.

The researchers propose a "polyclonal cascade" model: the emergence of one or a few initial self-reactive mutant clones facilitates the progressive incorporation of new mutant clones over time, gradually building an autoimmune response that becomes self-sustaining.

From Broad Suppression to Targeted Therapy

Autoimmune diseases currently affect 5 to 10% of the global population and are treated by broadly suppressing the immune system, which leaves patients vulnerable to infections and other complications. If the somatic mutation mechanism is confirmed across other autoimmune conditions, it could enable precision therapies targeting only the specific mutant cell populations.

"Autoimmune diseases are currently treated by broadly suppressing the immune system, which can leave patients vulnerable to infections. If these findings are confirmed, they could eventually enable more precise diagnoses and treatments."

— Dr Pantelis Nicola, NIHR Clinical Lecturer, The Christie, Manchester

The team has already begun observing similar mutation patterns in other autoimmune conditions, though these preliminary findings require further investigation.

Global Relevance

Thyroid autoimmunity is among the most common autoimmune conditions worldwide, with particularly high prevalence in South Asian populations. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the leading cause of hypothyroidism globally. For the Indian diaspora, the research offers hope that the cycle of lifelong immunosuppressive medication may eventually give way to treatments that address the root cause of disease rather than simply managing symptoms.

The study was supported by Wellcome and involved researchers from across the Cambridge Biomedical Campus and the NIHR Cambridge Biomedical Research Centre.
